lesson.title: Reading the Chain Rule as dy/du Times du/dx
lesson.summary: Leibniz notation turns the chain rule into a memorable pattern, dy/dx equals dy/du times du/dx, by naming the inside function u and tracking how a small change ripples through two nested relationships.
lesson.body:
Gottfried Leibniz built his calculus notation around the idea that a derivative describes a ratio of infinitesimal changes, dy over dx. That notation earns its keep most clearly in the chain rule, where a quantity y depends on x only through some intermediate quantity u. Writing dy/dx = dy/du times du/dx lets you see the composition in the notation itself: y changes with u, and u changes with x, so the two rates multiply. This is more than a notational convenience: physics and related rates problems are routinely written directly in terms of ratios such as dy/dx, dr/dt, and dV/dt, and Leibniz notation lets those ratios be chained together algebraically without ever leaving the language of rates.

Formally, if y = f(u) and u = g(x), the Leibniz chain rule states dy/dx = (dy/du)(du/dx). This is the same statement as the prime notation version, (f(g(x)))' = f'(g(x)) g'(x); it is not a new rule, just a different bookkeeping system. The advantage of Leibniz notation is that it makes substitution explicit: you literally rename the inside function u, differentiate the outside expression with respect to u, differentiate u with respect to x, then multiply. Keeping track of where each piece is evaluated matters: dy/du is found while treating u as the variable, du/dx is found while treating x as the variable, and only after both pieces exist does substituting u = g(x) back in turn the answer into a function of x again.

Let y = (3x + 1)^5. Set u = 3x + 1, so y = u^5. Then dy/du = 5u^4 and du/dx = 3. Leibniz's formula gives dy/dx = 5u^4 times 3 = 15u^4 = 15(3x+1)^4. Check this against the prime notation chain rule applied directly to the original expression: with f(t) = t^5 and g(x) = 3x+1, f'(t) = 5t^4 so f'(g(x)) = 5(3x+1)^4, and g'(x) = 3, giving f'(g(x))g'(x) = 15(3x+1)^4. Both routes land on exactly the same derivative. A second example reinforces the substitution habit: for y = sqrt(x^3+2), set u = x^3+2 so y = u^(1/2). Then dy/du = (1/2)u^(-1/2) and du/dx = 3x^2, so dy/dx = (1/2)(x^3+2)^(-1/2) times 3x^2 = 3x^2 / (2 sqrt(x^3+2)), the same answer that direct application of the power chain rule would produce on the original expression without ever naming u.

It helps to know why the cancel the du heuristic works even though du and dx are not literally numbers you can divide. Each derivative dy/du and du/dx is a limit of a difference quotient, and the chain rule is proved by multiplying and dividing an intermediate difference quotient by the change in u, then taking limits carefully. The notation is suggestive precisely because the proof, in spirit, really does involve multiplying two ratios of small changes together. The pattern extends to longer chains too: if y depends on u, u depends on v, and v depends on x, then dy/dx = (dy/du)(du/dv)(dv/dx), a preview of the layered reasoning used later when three or more functions are nested inside one another.

The practical payoff shows up once you start using u substitution to identify inside functions, the same skill developed in recognizing composition. Whenever an expression is a function of a function, naming the inner piece u turns a possibly confusing derivative into two easy ones multiplied together, dy/du and du/dx, exactly the mechanism this course leans on for every chain rule variant that follows: powers, trig, exponentials, and logarithms. Students who get comfortable writing out u explicitly, rather than trying to differentiate everything in one mental leap, tend to make far fewer sign and factor errors once the expressions get longer.
